section.title: Mourning for the One They Pierced
section.sectionRationale: The second burden opens on the day of the LORD. The nations gather against Jerusalem, but the God who stretches out the heavens makes the city an immovable stone that shatters all who lift it. Then, at the heart of the deliverance, comes the most piercing line of the book: the LORD pours out a spirit of grace, and His people look on Me, the One they have pierced, and mourn. John hears the cross in these words.
section.thesis: The LORD who defends Jerusalem against the nations wounds His people more deeply with grace than the sword ever could, opening their eyes to the One they pierced so that they mourn in repentance and are saved.
section.frameNote: Two movements: Jerusalem made an immovable stone that breaks the gathered nations, the weakest defender like David and the house of David like God; and the outpoured spirit of grace that makes the city look on the pierced One and mourn, clan by clan, for an only Son.

units.label: Jerusalem, an immovable stone
units.note: the nations broken on the city of God

verses.text: This is the burden of the word of the LORD concerning Israel. Thus declares the LORD, who stretches out the heavens and lays the foundation of the earth, who forms the spirit of man within him:
“Behold, I will make Jerusalem a cup of drunkenness to all the surrounding peoples. Judah will be besieged, as well as Jerusalem.
On that day, when all the nations of the earth gather against her, I will make Jerusalem a {{even|heavy stone}} for all the peoples; all who would heave it away will be severely injured.

On that day, declares the LORD, I will strike every horse with panic, and every rider with madness. I will keep a watchful eye on the house of Judah, but I will strike with blindness all the horses of the nations.
Then the leaders of Judah will say in their hearts: ‘The people of Jerusalem are my strength, for the LORD of Hosts is their God.’

On that day I will make the clans of Judah like a firepot in a woodpile, like a flaming torch among the sheaves; they will consume all the peoples around them on the right and on the left, while the people of Jerusalem remain secure there.
The LORD will save the tents of Judah first, so that the glory of the house of David and of the people of Jerusalem may not be greater than that of Judah.
On that day the LORD will defend the people of Jerusalem, so that the weakest among them will be like David, and the house of David will be like God, like the angel of the LORD going before them.
So on that day I will set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem.

units.label: Mourning the One they pierced
units.note: a spirit of grace and bitter repentance

verses.text: Then I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem a spirit of {{chen|grace}} and prayer, and they will look on Me, the One they have {{daqar|pierced}}. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an {{yachid|only child}}, and grieve bitterly for Him as one grieves for a firstborn son.
On that day the wailing in Jerusalem will be as great as the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo.
The land will mourn, each clan on its own: the clan of the house of David and their wives, the clan of the house of Nathan and their wives,
the clan of the house of Levi and their wives, the clan of Shimei and their wives,
and all the remaining clans and their wives.

even.gloss: A heavy or burdensome stone. The picture is of a boulder too great to lift; every nation that tries to heave Jerusalem away only ruptures itself in the effort. The city is not strong in itself but is made immovable by the God who forms it, so that the weight of the world's hostility falls back on those who raise it.

chen.gloss: Grace, favor, unmerited kindness. The LORD pours out a spirit of grace and prayer, a Spirit-wrought softening that turns hard hearts toward repentance. It is grace that opens the eyes, grace that produces the mourning; the tears of verse 10 are not the root of salvation but its fruit, drawn out by the freely given favor of God.

daqar.gloss: To pierce or thrust through, as with a sword or spear. The stunning offense of the verse is that the LORD says they pierced Me, yet then mourn for Him: the God of Israel identifies Himself with the pierced One. John 19:37 cites this word of the spear thrust into the crucified Jesus, reading the pierced LORD of Zechariah as the Son on the cross.

yachid.gloss: An only one, an only child, the sole and beloved heir. The same word describes Isaac, Abraham's only son. The mourning for the pierced One is the deepest grief a family can know, the loss of the only child and the firstborn, a sorrow the New Testament sees answered in the only begotten Son given up for sinners.

basic.context: The second of Zechariah's two closing burdens turns to the day of the LORD. The nations of the earth mass against Jerusalem, but God makes the city a cup that makes her attackers stagger and a stone that crushes all who try to lift it. He strikes the enemy cavalry with panic and blindness, and He makes the weakest defender fight like David. Then, in the middle of the rescue, comes the turn no one expects: God pours out a spirit of grace, and the people look on the One they pierced and weep for Him like parents weeping over an only child, family by family, across the whole land.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prophecy of the day of the LORD, wrapped in the recurring phrase on that day. Some of it looks to God's protection of His people in history, but its center, the pierced One and the mourning, is read by the New Testament as fulfilled in Christ. The great debate is whether the chapter describes a still future turning of ethnic Israel to Jesus, or the ingathering of God's people more broadly; either way, the piercing points to the cross.
basic.originalLanguages: Jerusalem is made an even ma'amasah, a heavy stone that injures all who heave it. Salvation comes when God pours out chen, grace, a Spirit-given favor that opens blind eyes. They look on the One they daqar, pierced, the very word John uses of the spear in Jesus' side, and they mourn for Him as for a yachid, an only child, the word used of Isaac, Abraham's only son.
basic.typology: The pierced One mourned as an only child prefigures Christ, the only begotten Son, pierced on the cross and looked upon in faith. The immovable stone that breaks the nations anticipates the stone the builders rejected, which became the cornerstone and the crushing stone of judgment. The outpoured spirit of grace looks ahead to Pentecost and the Spirit who convicts the world of sin.
basic.christ: John 19:37 quotes this verse over the crucified Jesus: they will look on the One they have pierced. Zechariah's astonishing grammar, where the LORD says they pierced Me yet then mourn for Him, is answered in the incarnation: the God of Israel was pierced in the flesh of His Son. The mourning for an only child is the sorrow of those who see what they did to the beloved Son, and it is met not with wrath but with an opened fountain in the next chapter.
basic.god: God is the Creator who stretches out the heavens and forms the human spirit, and He bends all of that power to defend His people and to save them. But His deepest work is not the shattering of the nations; it is the pouring out of grace that breaks hard hearts. He wounds His people with mercy, granting them the gift of repentance, and He so identifies with the pierced One that their sin against Him becomes the doorway to their salvation.
basic.crossReferences: John 19:37 cites the piercing, fulfilled at the cross. Revelation 1:7 says every eye will see Him, including those who pierced Him, and all will mourn. Romans 11 speaks of a future turning of Israel to Christ. Acts 2 shows a crowd in Jerusalem cut to the heart and calling on the Lord.
basic.oneStory: The nations rage against the city of God, but God defends her and, better still, saves her by grace. The turning point of history is a look at the pierced One and a flood of repentant tears. That look is fixed at Golgotha, where the God of Israel, in His Son, is pierced for our transgressions, and where the mourning of the guilty becomes the beginning of their joy.

context.literary:
Zechariah 9 to 14 is made of two oracles, each headed by the same word, massa, "burden" (9:1 and 12:1). This second burden is built as a diptych. Verses 1 to 9 face outward: the nations mass against Jerusalem, and the refrain "on that day" drives the action through verses 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9 as God turns one image after another against the attackers. Verses 10 to 14 face inward. The hinge is a single "then" at verse 10, where the subject changes from what God does to the enemy to what God does to His own people. The mood changes with it, from military triumph to a funeral.

Verse 1 prepares both halves by naming God with three participles: He stretches out the heavens, lays the earth's foundation, and forms the spirit of man within him. The first two guarantee the battle; the third guarantees the pouring out of verse 10, because the One who made the human spirit is the One who can remake it.

The images in verses 2 to 6 grow smaller and fiercer: a cup that makes the drinker stagger, a boulder that wounds the lifter, a firepot in a woodpile, a torch among sheaves. Verse 7 shows an unusual order of rescue, the tents of Judah first, so that the house of David and the city do not boast over the countryside. Verse 8 then lifts the weakest to David's stature and the house of David to a station "like God, like the angel of the LORD."

The lament of verses 11 to 14 is arranged with care. Four named clans appear in two pairs, the royal line (David and Nathan) and the Levitical line (Levi and Shimei), then "all the remaining clans," each mourning apart, and the wives are named separately every time. The whole community is grieving, and not one household is left out.
context.historical:
Chapters 9 to 14 carry no date, unlike Zechariah 1 to 8, which are anchored in 520 to 518 BC. They are most naturally read as addressed to the same small community in Persian Judah, a province with a rebuilt temple (finished in 516 BC, Ezra 6:15), no king, and a horizon of one imperial power after another. Hearers who had watched Babylon fall to Persia knew how quickly the cavalry of great empires could come and go, and so the picture of horses struck with panic and riders with madness (12:4) would have landed against a very real fear.

The shape of the battle is not new to Zechariah. It draws on the old Zion songs and prophecies in which the nations gather against the city of God and are broken before it can fall: Psalms 46, 48 and 76, and Isaiah 29:1-8. The people who heard it were being told that their small city belonged to that story.

The House of David mattered a great deal at this moment. The line had no throne, and hopes had gathered around Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23) and then faded. Naming the house of David and the people of Jerusalem as the first to receive the spirit of grace places the royal family at the head of the repentance, not the head of the victory. Nathan, who appears in verse 12, is either the prophet who confronted David (2 Samuel 12) or David's son of that name (2 Samuel 5:14, Luke 3:31); the Hebrew does not say which. Shimei is a grandson of Levi through Gershon (Numbers 3:17-18).

The wailing of Hadad-rimmon at Megiddo is debated. Many take it as the national grief at the death of the good king Josiah in the plain of Megiddo, a mourning for which Jeremiah composed laments that were still sung (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). Others see a reference to a mourning rite for a storm god of that name. Either way the comparison is to the deepest and most public grief the region knew.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a family of texts in which the nations gather against Jerusalem and are broken: Joel 3, Ezekiel 38 and 39, and Isaiah 29 and 17:12-14. Zechariah gives that family a surprising center. Where the others end with the enemy's defeat, this one ends with Israel's heartbreak and repentance.

The same verse can be read backward and forward. Backward, the phrase "pour out" is the language of Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28, where God pours out His Spirit on His people. The mourning for an only child echoes Amos 8:10, where God threatens a day like the grief of losing an only son, and Jeremiah 6:26. Here the same grief is turned from judgment into the doorway of grace.

Forward, the New Testament uses this chapter more than almost any other. John 19:37 quotes verse 10 over the cross, and the BSB footnote marks the citation. Revelation 1:7 echoes it with every eye seeing Him and the tribes of the earth mourning, and Matthew 24:30 uses the same mourning of the tribes in the Olivet discourse. The pouring out of the Spirit at Pentecost is described in the same verb in Acts 2:33, and Hebrews 10:29 names the Spirit who is insulted by apostasy the "Spirit of grace," the title Zechariah gives Him here.

Paul's argument in Romans 11:25-27 about the salvation of "all Israel" is often read alongside this chapter, though he does not quote it. So is the crowd on Pentecost, cut to the heart in Jerusalem (Acts 2:36-37), the first visible response to a sermon that tells the city it killed its Lord.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Zechariah meant a fragile community to take two lessons together. The first is that they do not have to be the strongest city to be a safe one: the God who made the heavens and the earth has made Himself Jerusalem's shield, and the forces they dread, the horses and chariots of empire, are in His hand. They are free to stand without panic.

The second lesson is harder and more important. The deepest danger in the chapter is not outside the walls. Even after the enemy is beaten, something must happen inside the city, and no army can do it. A spirit of grace must be poured out, and only then do the leaders of the people look at the One they have wounded and weep. The prophet wanted the hearers to understand that repentance is itself God's gift, that it begins in sight (they look) before it becomes sorrow (they mourn), and that it reaches every family and every rank. Nobody is excused from the weeping, from the throne to the temple, and nobody is shut out of the grace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is almost entirely a promise, with no command in it. God says what He will do: make the city a stone, strike the cavalry, pour out the Spirit. A reader should not turn the battle scenes into a program, as though believers were to arm themselves in the name of Jerusalem, because nothing here is a call to fight. The weapon in the passage is God Himself.

What is prescriptive by implication is the pattern of the mourning. The way the chapter describes true repentance, with each clan weeping apart, no public performance, no shortcut, is a model for how a community should turn when the Spirit shows it what it has done. It also tells a church how to treat its own sin: honest grief that comes from seeing Christ, and not from fear of punishment, and grief that is shared but also personal.

debates.question: Who is the pierced One, and how does the shift from Me to Him work?

views.label: The LORD Himself, pierced in the person of the Son
views.case: The speaker is the LORD, who says they will look on Me whom they pierced, and then the sentence slides into the third person, mourn for Him. Christian readers have long taken this as the incarnation in advance: the God of Israel wounded in the flesh of the Messiah. John 19:37 names the crucifixion as the fulfillment.

views.label: The LORD's representative, so closely bound to Him that his wounding is God's
views.case: Some read the pierced One as a messenger or shepherd so identified with God that the attack on him is an attack on the LORD. They note that a number of Hebrew manuscripts read look to him rather than look on Me, and that the verb for pierce is also used of killing a person (Numbers 25:8, Judges 9:54).

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the center: the wound is real, God owns it as His own, and the gaze of repentance is fixed there. The New Testament settles the identity by pointing to Jesus.

debates.question: Does the mourning describe a future turning of ethnic Israel, or the wider people of God?

views.label: A future national repentance of Israel
views.case: Read with Romans 11:25-27 and the repeated naming of the house of David, Nathan, Levi and Shimei, the passage foretells a day when the Jewish people, led by their leaders, look to their pierced Messiah and are saved family by family.

views.label: The ingathering of all God's people to the crucified Christ
views.case: Others hear the pattern already begun at Pentecost (Acts 2:36-37) and continuing wherever the Spirit turns hearts to the pierced Lord, Jew and Gentile alike, until every eye sees Him as Revelation 1:7 says.

debates.bearing: Either way the saving look is at Christ crucified and the response is Spirit-given mourning that leads to cleansing (13:1), not despair.

debates.question: What is the wailing of Hadad-rimmon?

views.label: The national lament for King Josiah
views.case: Josiah was killed at Megiddo, and the whole nation mourned him, with laments that were still sung long after (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). The place name Megiddo fits, and the comparison is to the most famous public grief in Judah's memory.

views.label: A mourning rite for a dying god of storm and fertility
views.case: Hadad and Rimmon are names of a Syrian storm god, and some see the verse comparing Jerusalem's grief to a seasonal weeping ritual of that kind, much as Ezekiel 8:14 mentions women weeping for Tammuz. The text does not explain itself either way.

debates.bearing: The point does not depend on settling it. Zechariah picks the biggest grief his hearers could imagine as the measure of how deeply the sight of the pierced One will cut.

study.originalLanguages:
Five words and constructions carry the weight of this chapter.

Massa, "burden" (12:1). From the verb nasa, "to lift," it can mean a load carried or a message lifted up and delivered. The same word heads Zechariah 9:1 and Malachi 1:1, and it often marks a heavy announcement about a nation. It is how the prophet signals that what follows is weighty and cannot be set down.

Shaphak, "pour out" (12:10). This verb is used for pouring out blood (Genesis 9:6), for pouring out wrath (Psalm 79:6), and, as here, for pouring out the Spirit (Ezekiel 39:29, Joel 2:28). The picture is of an abundance that cannot be rationed. It is never a drop; it is a deluge, and it falls on those who have done nothing to ask for it. The Spirit is poured on the house of David and the people of Jerusalem before they mourn, not after.

Chen and tachanunim, "grace" and "prayer" (12:10). The second word comes from the same root as the verb chanan, "to show favor," so the phrase is a spirit of favor and of cries for favor. The first gives the favor, and the second is the asking that favor makes possible. Moses used the first word when he said he had found grace in God's eyes (Exodus 33:12-17). Prayer is here not the cause of the outpouring but its fruit.

Daqar, "pierce" (12:10, also 13:3). It describes a thrust through the body, whether Phinehas driving a spear through Zimri and the woman (Numbers 25:8) or Abimelech asking his armor-bearer to run him through (Judges 9:54). It means a fatal wound, not a scratch. The word comes back in 13:3, where parents pierce their false-prophet son, and that echo ties the two chapters together. The Greek of John 19:37 uses ekkenteo, "to pierce through," which is a different verb from the one John uses in 19:34 for the spear thrust. John's wording is his own rendering of the Hebrew.

Yachid and bekhor, "only child" and "firstborn" (12:10). Yachid is the word God uses of Isaac when He tells Abraham to take his son, "your only son" (Genesis 22:2), and Amos uses it for the grief of losing an only child (Amos 8:10). The two words in tandem describe the loss of the one in whom a family's future rests: the only one, and the first of the family's strength.

A last small construction is the repeated "each clan" of verse 12, where the Hebrew doubles the noun to say family by family. The repetition itself slows the reading, as the grief does.

typology.type: The only child, Isaac, and the pierced Son
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah borrows the word yachid, the word God spoke of Isaac when He told Abraham to offer his only son, Genesis 22:2. That sets the pierced One in the line of the beloved son laid on the altar. Hebrews 11:17 calls Isaac Abraham's one and only son, and John 3:16 calls Jesus God's one and only Son. The escalation is plain: Isaac was spared, a ram taken in his place, but the Son of John 19 is pierced in fact. The type falls short because Isaac's sacrifice was stopped, and Jesus' was finished.

The city that wounds every hand that tries to lift it prefigures the stone of Matthew 21:44, on which anyone who falls is broken and on whom it falls is crushed, and the cornerstone of 1 Peter 2:6-8. It also echoes the stone cut without hands in Daniel 2:34-35 that breaks the statue of the nations. The fulfillment is that the stone is a person, Christ, in whom the city of God is gathered, Hebrews 12:22. The type falls short because Zechariah's stone is a place and a people. Only in the gospel does the stone have a heart that can break for His enemies.

Verse 8 promises that the weakest in Jerusalem will be like David, and that David's house will stand like the angel of the LORD. The Davidic line is lifted in the Son of David, Matthew 1:1 and 22:41-45, who is also David's Lord. The weak share in His strength by faith, which is the pattern of 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 where power is perfected in weakness. The type falls short because the house of David is only said to be like God. In Christ the likeness becomes an identity, and believers are made sharers in His life, not His equals.

The families of David, Nathan, Levi and Shimei each weeping apart are a first picture of the response to the crucified Lord. It appears in the Jerusalem women who followed Jesus mourning and wailing for Him, Luke 23:27-28, and in the crowd of Acts 2:37 cut to the heart. Revelation 1:7 widens it to all the tribes of the earth. The type is only partly fulfilled: those who wept at the cross did not yet understand it, and Jesus told them to weep for themselves. The mourning of Zechariah 12 is complete only when sorrow gives way to the fountain of 13:1.

study.christ:
John does not simply borrow a phrase. At the foot of the cross, after describing the soldier's spear and the flow of blood and water (19:34), he steps out of the narrative to say that "the one who saw it has testified to this," and then he sets two Scriptures beside the event. The second is this verse: "They will look on the One they have pierced." What John wants his reader to do is the thing Zechariah promised: to look. The Gospel ends its account of the crucifixion by inviting a gaze.

The grammar of the prophecy is what makes it christological. The speaker is the LORD, and He says they pierced Me. Then the pronoun changes and they mourn for Him. If the shift is deliberate, it describes One who can be both God and a person God's people can wound, and that is exactly what the New Testament says about Jesus: the Word who was God became flesh (John 1:14), so that the Lord of glory could be crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8). Isaiah 53:5 uses a different word but describes the same wound: He was pierced for our transgressions. Zechariah says who was pierced and who did it. Isaiah says why.

The mourning is for an only son and a firstborn, two titles that belong to Christ. He is the one and only Son (John 3:16), and He is the firstborn over all creation and from the dead (Colossians 1:15, 18). The look that Zechariah describes also echoes Numbers 21:8-9, where those bitten in the wilderness looked at the lifted serpent and lived, which Jesus applies to Himself in John 3:14-15.

The Spirit of grace who is poured out is the Spirit whom the risen Christ pours out from the Father's right hand (Acts 2:33). The order is the order of the gospel: the Spirit is given, eyes are opened, the cross is seen, sorrow comes, and sorrow is met by cleansing. Paul says that godly sorrow leads to repentance without regret (2 Corinthians 7:10).

A caution is needed. Zechariah does not name a spear, and the verse should not be reduced to a single proof text for an event. John sees it fulfilled in the cross as a whole, and the passage also stretches beyond the cross, to a looking and mourning still to come (Revelation 1:7). Nor does the text assign guilt to a single people: the weeping house of David and the people of Jerusalem are the first to receive grace, and elsewhere the New Testament says Jew and Gentile together gathered against God's anointed (Acts 4:27).
study.god:
The chapter opens with God's credentials, and they are not those of a tribal deity. He stretches out the heavens, founds the earth, and forms the human spirit. A God like that has no rival, and so the nations massed against Jerusalem are not a threat to His plan but tools in it: He is the one who gathers them (12:9 says He sets out to destroy those who come), and the cup of staggering and the boulder are things He makes.

The first half shows a God who uses weakness on purpose. He strikes horses with panic and riders with madness, so the strongest weapons of the empire are turned against themselves. He saves the tents of Judah before the city so that no one in the city will think itself better than the villages. He makes the weakest like David. God's way of winning is to scatter the proud and honor the lowly, and the order of the rescue in verse 7 is a small picture of the same principle.

The second half is where the doctrine of God deepens. Nothing in the first nine verses prepares us for the fact that the real battle is with hearts, and the one weapon that works is a gift. God pours out a spirit of grace and prayer. Repentance is not extracted by force, and it is not a human achievement. The same God who forms the spirit of man within him is the One who reforms it. That is a sovereign grace, and it is also tender: the people He rescues are not scolded into sorrow but given sight.

Most striking is the way God speaks of Himself. He says they pierced Me. God identifies so closely with the wounded One that the wound is His own. The tradition that has worked hardest at this verse will not say God suffers in His divine nature, but it will say that in the incarnation God the Son truly suffered in the flesh He took, and this verse is a sign that God's heart was already set that way: that He would let His people wound Him, and that He would turn their wounding into their healing.

For worship this does two things. It gives believers a reason to confess openly. Mourning in this chapter is not morbid; it is what happens to people who have seen the love of the One they hurt. And it gives them courage in the face of the powers of the world, because the One who holds the heavens in His hand is the same One who stoops to be pierced.

crossReferences.note: The cross is where John sees this verse come true. He names the spear, the blood and water, and then two Scriptures, one of which is Zechariah's look on the One they pierced. John's concern is that the reader will see and believe, the same two verbs that run through Zechariah's gaze.

John gathers the verse into the return of Christ: every eye will see Him, even those who pierced Him, and the tribes of the earth will mourn. The mourning of Zechariah is both a work of grace at the first coming and a recognition that widens at the second.

The word for only child, yachid, is the word used of Isaac. Abraham was told to take his only son, whom he loved. Zechariah's mourning for an only child sets the pierced One in this line, with the difference that for Isaac a ram was found, and for the pierced One no substitute is.

Amos turned the grief of losing an only son into a threat: God will make the people's feasts like mourning for an only son. Zechariah takes the same picture and uses it for the end of that mourning: grief that heals rather than grief that judges.

The death of Josiah at Megiddo and the laments sung for him ever after are the most likely background of the wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. The good king was killed in the plain, and Judah mourned. Zechariah says that grief will be small beside the grief for a greater King.

Here God promises to pour out His Spirit on all people. Zechariah 12:10 uses the same verb for the same gift, but pours it on the house of David and the people of Jerusalem first. Peter's sermon at Pentecost quotes Joel, and the crowd in Jerusalem is the first to mourn.

Peter tells the city that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ, the man they crucified. The people are cut to the heart and ask what to do. It is a first fulfillment of the mourning, in the same city, with the same pattern: the Spirit given, the crucified One seen, and the heart broken.

Isaiah uses a different word for pierced, but the wound is the same. He was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities. Zechariah says the people pierced Him. Isaiah says it was for them. The two together are the gospel in a sentence.

On the way to the cross women follow Jesus mourning and wailing for Him, and He turns and tells them to weep for themselves and their children. The scene shows the difference between sorrow at suffering and the repentance Zechariah promises, which comes only when the Spirit of grace opens the eyes.

The writer calls the Spirit the Spirit of grace, the very title Zechariah uses. To insult Him is to trample the Son and profane the blood of the covenant. The passage shows how seriously Scripture takes the gift that leads Zechariah's mourners to repentance: it cannot be turned aside lightly.

study.oneStory:
Everything in the chapter answers a question that began in a garden. When Adam and Eve hid from God in Genesis 3, the movement was away from Him: they ran, covered themselves, shifted blame. Zechariah describes the reversal. A people who have wounded God turn and look at Him. Hiding becomes gazing. The distance sin opened is closed from God's side, because the Spirit has to be poured out before anyone can turn.

The chapter also reaches back to the nations' attack on Zion that runs through the Psalms and the prophets, and it says the real war has never been the one with the nations. It is the war inside the people who are being defended. The prophets before Zechariah kept announcing judgment on Jerusalem for the sins of her leaders, the house of David first among them. Zechariah's answer is that the leaders will be the first to weep and the first to receive.

The line forward runs straight to the cross, where the look is fixed. Zechariah does not say how the One would be pierced, only that He would be, and that the people who pierced Him would be forgiven. The Gospels show how: a man on a cross, a spear, a flow of blood and water, a centurion's confession, crowds beating their breasts (Luke 23:47-48), and then Pentecost, in the same city, with the Spirit poured out and the heart of the city broken.

And it points on to the end. Revelation 1:7 pictures every eye seeing Him, and the tribes of the earth mourning. In the new creation no one will mourn from fear, because the One once wounded will be the One who wipes away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The mourning of Zechariah 12 is where that story takes its turn: sorrow over sin, the gift of the Spirit, and the beginning of cleansing in the very next verse, where a fountain is opened for sin and impurity.

quiz.q: What does God make Jerusalem for the gathered nations?

options.text: A cup of drunkenness and an immovable, heavy stone that injures all who try to lift it.
options.note: Verses 2 and 3 make the city a staggering cup and a burdensome stone.

options.text: An easy prize quickly overrun.
options.note: The opposite: the nations are broken on her, not victorious over her.

options.text: A place God abandons to the enemy.
options.note: God defends the city; He does not abandon it.

options.text: A neutral bystander in the conflict.
options.note: Jerusalem is the very stone that shatters her attackers.

quiz.q: What does God pour out that brings the people to repentance?

options.text: A spirit of grace and prayer that opens their eyes to the pierced One.
options.note: Verse 10: the mourning is the fruit of an outpoured spirit of grace.

options.text: A spirit of fear that terrifies them into silence.
options.note: It is grace, not mere terror, that produces the saving mourning.

options.text: Wealth and comfort so they forget their guilt.
options.note: The passage produces honest grief over sin, not distraction from it.

options.text: Nothing; they repent entirely on their own.
options.note: Repentance here is a Spirit-given gift, poured out by God.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use the words about the pierced One?

options.text: John 19:37 applies them to the crucified Jesus, whose side was pierced.
options.note: John cites this verse as fulfilled at the cross.

options.text: They are said to be fulfilled in a battle of the Maccabees.
options.note: The New Testament ties them to Christ crucified, not to that conflict.

options.text: They are treated as a mere figure of speech with no fulfillment.
options.note: John reads them as a real prophecy fulfilled in Jesus.

options.text: They are applied to the destruction of Rome.
options.note: John applies the piercing to Jesus on the cross.

quiz.q: How deep is the mourning over the pierced One?

options.text: As deep as grief for an only child and a firstborn son.
options.note: Verse 10 compares it to mourning an only child, the word used of Isaac.

options.text: A brief and passing sadness.
options.note: The grief is the deepest a family can know, not passing.

options.text: Only a formal, outward ritual with no feeling.
options.note: It is heartfelt, Spirit-wrought grief, clan by clan.

options.text: No real sorrow at all.
options.note: The whole land mourns bitterly, family by family.

quiz.q: What is the astonishing thing about who was pierced?

options.text: The LORD says they pierced Me, yet they mourn for Him, fulfilled as God pierced in His Son.
options.note: The shift from Me to Him is answered in the incarnation and the cross.

options.text: It was only a symbolic wound with no real person in view.
options.note: The New Testament sees a real piercing fulfilled in the real Jesus.

options.text: The one pierced was a foreign king.
options.note: The pierced One is identified with the LORD Himself, fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: No one is actually pierced in the passage.
options.note: The text plainly speaks of the One they have pierced.

questions: God made a weak city an immovable stone. Where do you need to trust that your safety rests in God rather than in your own strength?
The saving turn was a look at the pierced One. Have you truly looked on Christ crucified, or only glanced past the cross?
The mourning here is Spirit-given grace, not mere guilt. How does it change repentance to know that even your sorrow for sin is a gift from God?
They grieved for the pierced One as for an only child. Does your sin ever move you to that kind of honest grief, and then to His mercy?
God turned the wound His people inflicted into the source of their cleansing. Where do you need to believe that God can redeem even your worst failures?

translationNotes.note: Heavy stone renders even ma'amasah, a burdensome boulder; the image is of a weight too great to lift, so that all who heave it are ruptured in the effort.

The Hebrew reads look on Me, the One they have pierced, then shifts to mourn for Him; a few witnesses read look to the one, but the received text and John 19:37 support the reading that identifies the pierced One with the LORD Himself.
The wailing of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo likely recalls the national mourning over the death of good King Josiah, a byword for deep public grief.
